title: Citrobacter freundii bacteremia from pyelonephritis, afebrile and improving on ceftriaxone

clinical_review.notes: Owner approved revision 2 of the M6 library-growth draft (with OpenEvidence's review).

story: A 58-year-old man with acute pyelonephritis and Citrobacter freundii bacteremia (urine and blood, same susceptibilities) has been on IV ceftriaxone since admission. On hospital day 4 he has been afebrile for 48 hours, his vital signs are normal and he is eating; ultrasound shows no obstruction or abscess, and repeat blood cultures from day 2 have no growth. Prostatitis is not suspected: no prostatic tenderness and no urinary retention.

expected_findings.summary: Citrobacter freundii bacteremia on ceftriaxone, afebrile and improving: generally avoided for an AmpC organism; completing an empirically started course may be reasonable if non-severe, improving and source controlled.
Clinically stable with susceptible oral non-beta-lactams (ciprofloxacin, TMP-SMX), which also avoid the AmpC question.

reference_answer: Prefer oral step-down to ciprofloxacin 500 to 750 mg every 12 hours or TMP-SMX 160/800 mg every 12 hours, which are not AmpC substrates (IDSA 2026 Question 2.7) and resolve both findings, for 7 days of effective therapy counting the ceftriaxone days (IDSA 2025 cUTI with bacteremia). Changing to cefepime is the next choice. Completing ceftriaxone is defensible but least preferred: it was started empirically and the infection is non-severe, improving and source controlled (IDSA 2026 Question 2.4).
acceptable_answers: Oral step-down to ciprofloxacin 500 to 750 mg every 12 hours or TMP-SMX 160/800 mg every 12 hours, 7 days of effective therapy in total (preferred).
Change ceftriaxone to cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours (adjusted for renal function), then oral step-down when appropriate.
Complete the course with ceftriaxone given the empiric start, clinical improvement and source control (least preferred).
rationale: Tests the second AmpC organism end to end, the AmpC exception wording when there is no fever, and IV to PO in Gram-negative bacteremia with the AmpC note. Ambiguous because all three answers are defensible, in the order given (owner review, 2026-11-12). Prostatitis is excluded in the story because IDSA 2025 allows 10 to 14 days when it is suspected.

citations.supports: Questions 2.3, 2.4 and 2.7: cefepime preferred, the empiric-ceftriaxone exception, oral non-beta-lactam transition for AmpC organisms; checked against IDSA's 2026 text 2026-11-12.
